draft.title: Opportunity cost
card: Resources are scarce, so choosing one option means giving up others. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best option given up.

It is only the single next best option, not every option left behind. It is not always money: time, land or effort can be what is given up. A student who studies instead of working a shift gives up the wage they would have earned, if working was the next best option.
A trade-off is the act of giving up one thing to get another. Weighing the opportunity cost shows what each choice really costs.
In a cost-benefit analysis, a person or government compares the costs and benefits of a choice. A choice is worth making when its benefits outweigh its costs, including the opportunity cost.
draft.remember: Every choice has a cost: the next best option you gave up.

a.q: Mia has a free Saturday. She could work a shift for $120, go to the beach, or study. She chooses the beach and ranks studying second. What is her opportunity cost?
opts: The study time she gave up
The study time and the $120 together
The cost of getting to the beach
a.why: Opportunity cost is the next best option given up, and for Mia that is studying. The $120 shift was a third choice, so it is not counted. Adding it would count more than the single next best option.
a.clue: Which option did she rank second?

b.q: Dubbo council has land for one project. It could build a library, which it ranks first, a car park, which it ranks second, or a skate park, which it ranks third. What is the opportunity cost of choosing the library?
opts: The car park and the skate park
Nothing, as the library was its first choice
b.why: The opportunity cost is the next best option given up, which is the car park. The skate park is also given up but ranks lower, so it is not counted. Choosing the best option still has an opportunity cost, because something is given up.
b.clue: Does making the best choice mean nothing at all is given up?

a.best: The study time she gave up
